label: contraction · de + os (masc. plural)
scene: Several things coming away from a group, down from that source.
definition_pt: De + os: “Eu sou dos Estados Unidos.”
origin: de + os fused into one word. Portuguese merges prepositions with articles all the time (do, da, no, na, pelo).
notes: Contraction of de + os (masc. plural). E.g. "dos Estados Unidos." | Many countries take an article: o Brasil → do Brasil; os Estados Unidos → dos Estados Unidos. But Portugal has none: de Portugal.

label: plural
scene: A hand holding a small fold of twenty-dollar notes, more than one bill in the fingers.
definition_pt: Mais de um dólar: “vinte dólares”.
root_image: The same valley silver, now a sheaf of notes in the hand.
origin: the same German Thaler / Joachimsthaler name, in the Portuguese plural. Regular -es plural after a consonant-final loan: dólar → dólares (the accent stays on the same syllable, written on the ó).
notes: Word history: from German Thaler, from Joachimsthaler (a silver coin of Joachimsthal).

label: você · you want
scene: The other person's hands stretch toward it, reaching.
definition_pt: Pergunta, ou diz, se a outra pessoa quer uma coisa.
root_image: The same seeking root as eu quero, now on the other side: their hands going after the thing.
parts_meaning: quer is the 3rd-person present of querer; você takes 3rd-person verbs because it comes from Vossa Mercê, "Your Grace."
origin: The same Latin quaerere → querer as in eu quero. The 3rd-person present quer is used with você: você quer?
notes: Você quer? is the everyday question. O senhor quer? / A senhora quer? in formal address.

label: plural
scene: A Brazilian twenty-reais note, a golden lion tamarin on a branch, the words VINTE REAIS along the edge.
definition_pt: Mais de um real: “vinte reais”.
root_image: The same royal stamp, now on more than one coin or note.
literal: "royal ones" → the modern plural of the currency
parts_meaning: the modern plural of o real
origin: same Latin rēgālis "royal." The historical plural of the old real was réis, which was also the name of the currency for a long time (the réis / mil-réis). After 1994 the official plural is reais.
notes: Pronounced roughly "hey-ICE" in much of Brazil (initial r like English h). | Word history: from Latin rēgālis (royal).

label: eu · I know
origin: The 1st-person present is irregular: eu sei, not *sabo (compare Spanish sé, French sais, Italian so).
notes: Taught inside eu não sei (Lesson 5); not drilled on its own.

label: você · you know
definition_pt: Pergunta ou diz que a outra pessoa tem a informação: “Você sabe onde fica?”
root_image: The same tasting root as sei: the flavor is there this time. You have sampled it, and you know.

label: masculine · to a man
definition_pt: A forma educada de dizer “você” para um homem, quase sempre mais velho.

label: feminine · to a woman
scene: An elder woman with white hair; the room quiets and makes space.
definition_pt: A forma educada de dizer “você” para uma mulher, quase sempre mais velha.
root: feminine of senhor ← Latin seniōrem ‘the older one’
literal: "the elder lady" → respectful "you" for a woman
parts_meaning: a < Latin illam ("that one," fem.); -a marks feminine
origin: a feminine form of senhor. Latin had no special feminine of senior; Romance built one: Spanish señora, Italian signora, French madame uses a different root (ma dame < mea domina).

label: eu · I am
definition_pt: O que eu digo para falar quem ou o que eu sou: “Eu sou americano.”
literal: "I am" for identity, origin, profession. Eu sou americano. Eu sou fotógrafo.

label: ele / ela / você · is
scene: A stone set in the earth, simply there, by its nature.
definition_pt: Forma do verbo ser: “Ele é brasileiro.” “Você é americano.”
parts: single verb form (3rd person singular of ser)
origin: Latin est → é (final -st lost). "They are" = são < Latin sunt (final -nt → nasal -ão).
notes: "They are" is são. | The accent matters: é (open "eh") = "is"; e (no accent, "ee") = "and."

label: você · you are
scene: That same nod, then a quiet naming of who they are, as if speaking of someone a step apart from you.
definition_pt: Forma do verbo ser para “você”: “Você é brasileiro?”

label: masculine
notes: Reference form: not yet taught on its own.

label: eu · I have
definition_pt: Eu seguro uma coisa comigo; ela é minha.

label: você · you have
scene: Your hands close around something and keep it.
definition_pt: Pergunta ou diz que a outra pessoa tem alguma coisa: “Você tem uma mala?”
root_image: Latin tenēre = to hold, to keep in the hand and not let go. To have something is, at root, to hold it.
parts_meaning: tem is the 3rd-person present of ter, "to have"; você again takes the 3rd person.
origin: Latin tenēre "to hold, keep" became Portuguese ter. In classical Latin, habēre was the main verb for "to have," and tenēre was "to hold." Spanish still uses both (tener for possession, haber as auxiliary and existential). Older Portuguese also used haver for possession; over time ter took over "to have / to possess," and haver shrank mainly to the existential há ("there is") and some auxiliary uses (havia, haver de).

label: feminine
definition_pt: O número 1 com palavra feminina: “uma mala”.
root_image: The same single thing as um, now agreeing with a feminine noun.
parts_meaning: "one" and also "a / an," agreeing with a feminine noun (uma mala, uma senhora)
origin: Latin ūnam, the feminine of ūnus, became uma. Masculine um < ūnum.
